ⓐ.summary: The principal-agent problem arises for homeowners selling through real estate agents: agents induce quick sales at lower prices to save their own costs.

c1.text: When a principal cannot perfectly observe an agent's actions, the agent may maximize their own interests at the expense of the principal's interests (the principal-agent problem).

c2.text: The principal-agent problem arises for homeowners who sell their house through real estate agents.

c3.text: Real estate agents effectively receive only about 1.5% commission on the sale price.

c4.text: Obtaining a higher sale price requires keeping the property on the market longer and incurring extra costs for advertising and showings.

c5.text: For an additional $10,000 in sale price, the agent earns only an additional $150, which does not offset the extra costs of staying on the market longer.

c6.text: Rather than paying extra costs for a small commission increase, the agent is incentivized to sell the house relatively quickly at a reasonable price.

c7.text: Homeowners have far less information than agents regarding home value or sale likelihood, making them prone to accept the agent's suggestion to settle for a lower price.

h1.text: Agents leave their own properties on the market longer than those belonging to others.

h2.text: When selling their own properties, agents act as principals and hold out longer, showing that agents sell clients' homes quickly to serve their own interests.

a.note: When selling their own homes, agents face no principal-agent conflict and keep them on the market longer; this supports the claim that quick sales of clients' homes stem from the principal-agent problem.

h3.text: Increasing the effective commission rate from 1.5% to 3.5% led to homes spending less time on the market.

h4.text: A higher commission rate increases the marginal gain from a higher price and should lengthen time on the market; shortening time on the market contradicts the principal-agent explanation.

b.note: If ⓐ were correct, a higher commission rate would incentivize agents to keep homes on the market longer; the finding shows less time, conflicting with ⓐ rather than strengthening it.

h5.text: The development of information and communication technology, making housing price information easier and more accurate to obtain, has shortened the time homes spend on the market.

h6.text: Reduced information asymmetry enables homeowners to resist lower prices and keep homes on the market longer; shortening time on the market contradicts the principal-agent explanation.

c.note: If information asymmetry diminishes, homeowners are less prone to accept quick, lower-price sales, so time on market should increase; shortening time on the market conflicts with ⓐ rather than strengthening it.
